title: Long Days, Short Years
author: Nate Foster
summary: Nate Foster reflects on his son Hudson's wedding preparation and approaching independence, realizing eighteen years passed faster than expected despite feeling slow while happening. The blur from learning to walk through graduation teaches him the golden years appear golden only in hindsight. For parents in the thick of childhood chaos, embracing the unique, unrepeatable season matters more than waiting for clarity that comes only after it ends. Foster reminds parents that the fullness of those years becomes visible only in the rearview mirror, making presence now essential. The transition from childhood to adulthood happens in the everyday rituals and small moments, visible only when they become memories. What feels slow and endless in the moment becomes impossible to hold back in reflection.
points: Eighteen years moves from seeming long to impossibly short; watching Hudson move out reveals the compressed timeline of childhood development.
The golden years rarely feel golden while living them; parents mistake their overwhelm and tiredness as evidence they are failing when they are actually standing in the richest season.
Each season of parenting is unique and unrepeatable; embracing chaos and slowness now prevents the regret that comes from waiting for clarity visible only in the rearview mirror.
Foster's practice of checking if Hudson's car was in the driveway shows the small rituals that mark seasons of presence, soon to become memories.
The cycle continues as fathers become grandfathers, teaching men to steward generations rather than chase achievement in a single lifetime.
quotes: Eighteen years sounds like a long time. It isn't. All of it felt slow while it was happening. None of it feels slow now.
The days are long, but the years are short. From learning to walk through graduation, the blur of childhood passes faster than expected.
I know you're tired. I know you feel like you're failing some days. I know you feel overwhelmed. But the golden years usually don't look golden while you're in them.
Embrace it. It's short. It's unique. It doesn't come back.
